title: Mastery Challenge: Philosophy
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Philosophy Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: Questions from across the tree: the first traditions, beauty and art, death, the Stoics, meaning and the absurd. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Philosophy Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the tree, from Plato’s Forms to Sisyphus’s boulder. Level 1 asked what philosophy is; now show what it can do. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Philosophy: mastered
learned: How thinkers weigh beauty, death and meaning without claiming the last word.
Why Epicurus called death nothing to us, and what his critics say it takes away.
What Nozick’s machine, Nietzsche’s demon and Camus’s Sisyphus test about a good life.
How to take a new big question through clarifying, a thought experiment and rival views.

questions.prompt: A friend says the perfect circle of geometry is more real than any circle you can draw. Whose theory is that closest to?

options.label: Aristotle’s
options.rationale: Aristotle put form inside things, not above them.

options.label: The Carvaka materialists’
options.rationale: They trusted perception alone.

options.label: Laozi’s
options.rationale: The Dao isn’t a perfect shape.

questions.explanation: Plato held that the Forms, such as Circle, are more real than the changing things we see.

questions.prompt: A carpenter builds a chair so that people can sit on it. Which of Aristotle’s causes is “so people can sit”?

options.label: The material cause
options.rationale: That would be the wood.

options.label: The formal cause
options.rationale: That would be its shape.

options.label: The efficient cause
options.rationale: That would be the carpenter’s skill.

questions.explanation: The final cause is what a thing is for.

questions.prompt: How did Confucius change the meaning of junzi?

options.label: From a person of noble birth to a person of moral nobility
From a trained soldier to a learned scholar
options.rationale: The shift was from birth to character.

options.label: From a hereditary ruler to a humble servant
options.rationale: Not the change he made.

options.label: From a priest to a merchant
options.rationale: Not the change he made.

questions.explanation: Junzi first meant a prince’s son; Confucius made it a person of moral nobility from any background.

questions.prompt: What does Nagasena’s chariot show about a person, on the Buddhist argument?

options.label: A person is a lasting soul riding in a changing body
options.rationale: The argument denies any self over and above the parts.

options.label: A person is the single most important part, the mind
options.rationale: No single part is the self.

options.label: People are unreal in every sense
options.rationale: They’re conventionally real, like the chariot.

options.label: A person is a name for parts working together, with no self beyond them

questions.explanation: Like a chariot, a person is conventionally real: a name for parts well arranged, nothing more.

questions.prompt: Which classical Indian school accepted perception alone as a reliable source of knowledge?

options.label: Nyaya
options.rationale: Nyaya accepted four sources, including inference.

options.label: Advaita Vedanta
options.rationale: It focused on self and Brahman.

options.label: The Jains
options.rationale: They stressed that truth is many-sided.

questions.explanation: The Carvaka materialists trusted perception alone.

questions.prompt: Which thinker made the joint verdict of true critics the standard of taste?

options.label: Kant
options.rationale: Kant said beauty speaks with a universal voice.

options.label: Tolstoy
options.rationale: Tolstoy defined art by expression.

options.label: Nietzsche
options.rationale: Nietzsche criticized Kant’s view.

questions.explanation: Hume held that true critics, with delicate taste, practice and no prejudice, together set the standard.

questions.prompt: Nozick’s experience machine suggests that something matters besides experience. Which premise of Epicurus’s argument about death does that challenge?

options.label: The gods do not care about us
options.rationale: That isn’t a premise of this argument.

options.label: Death comes to everyone
options.rationale: Nozick doesn’t challenge that.

options.label: Fear of death is common
options.rationale: That’s not a premise either.

questions.explanation: If something matters besides experience, then good and bad don’t lie wholly in sensation, and Epicurus’s first premise is in doubt.

questions.prompt: A rival wins the prize you hoped for. Which response fits Epictetus best?

options.label: Demand that the judges change their decision
options.rationale: The decision was never up to you.

options.label: Examine your own view of the loss and set your next aim
Decide that effort is pointless
options.rationale: Epictetus urged effort, with composure.

options.label: Blame the rival for your distress
options.rationale: He said our views, not others, disturb us.

questions.explanation: The prize is beyond your power; your judgments and aims are within it.

questions.prompt: Someone loves collecting bottle caps and says that is all it takes for a meaningful life. Whose view agrees, and who objects?

options.label: Wolf agrees; Frankfurt objects
options.rationale: It’s the other way round.

options.label: Supernaturalists agree; subjectivists object
options.rationale: Supernaturalists look to God’s purpose.

options.label: Everyone agrees
options.rationale: The ball-of-string objection targets exactly this.

options.label: Subjectivists like Frankfurt agree; Wolf objects

questions.explanation: For Frankfurt, caring is what counts; Wolf insists what you care about must also be truly worthwhile.

questions.prompt: Nietzsche’s demon and Camus’s Sisyphus both picture endless repetition. What response do both thinkers praise?

options.label: Waiting patiently for a reward in a later life
options.rationale: Both rule out that escape.

options.label: Refusing to think about it
options.rationale: Both demand clear awareness.

options.label: Embracing this life with open eyes, with no escape
Hoping the repetition will stop one day
options.rationale: Neither offers that hope.

questions.explanation: Nietzsche asks for a yes to this life as it is; Camus asks for lucid revolt with no escape, and pictures Sisyphus happy.
